title: in the application by The North Harris Trust Applicant against Donald N M MacDonald Respondent [2025] SLC 11
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 11,
Case reference: SLC/47/24

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Lord Duthie,
Mr John Smith

in the application by
The North Harris Trust
Applicant
against
Donald N M MacDonald
Respondent

Subjects: Common Grazings, Township of Ardvourlie, Harris

26 September 2025

Introduction

[1] The applicant seeks to resume 3,180 square metres of common grazing at Ardvourlie, Harris in term of sections 20 and 21 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. The stated purpose of the resumption is to develop an Outdoor Hub, including a facilities building with café and retail space to support mountain biking and improve visitor infrastructure. Planning permission has been granted and preliminary works have commenced.

[2] The application is opposed by the respondent who is one of only two shareholders in the common grazing. Parties agreed that the court should determine the matter on the basis of written submissions.

The Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993

[3] The 1993 Act provides, inter alia, as follows:

“20 Resumption of croft or part of croft by landlord.

(1) The Land Court may, on the application of the landlord and on being satisfied that he desires to resume the croft, or part thereof, for some reasonable purpose having relation to the good of the croft or of the estate or to the public interest or the interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft, authorise the resumption thereof by the landlord upon such terms and conditions as it may think fit, and may require the crofter to surrender his croft, in whole or in part, to the landlord accordingly, upon the landlord making adequate compensation to the crofter either by letting to him other land of equivalent value in the neighbourhood or by compensation in money or by way of an adjustment of rent or in such other manner as the Land Court may determine.

…

21 Crofter’s right to share in value of land resumed by landlord.

(1) Where the Land Court authorises the resumption of a croft or a part thereof under section 20 of this Act, the crofter shall be entitled to receive from the landlord, in addition to any compensation payable to him under that section, a share in the value of the land so resumed the amount whereof shall be one half of the difference between, subject to subsection (5) below, the market value of the land (on the date on which resumption thereof is so authorised) as determined by the Land Court in accordance with subsections (2) and (3) below (less any compensation payable as aforesaid) and the crofting value thereof.”

Submissions for the applicant

[4] The proposed development is for a reasonable purpose. The development will enhance the visitor experience, benefit the wider community and economy and encourage responsible use of designated paths, thereby protecting the common pasture. Planning consent has been obtained. Initial works commenced in early 2023, maintaining the validity of the consent. These works include installation of services and an electric vehicle charge point, as well as ground preparation.

[5] The land is not actively grazed. Sufficient alternative grazing is available.

[6] Compensation of £250 was previously agreed with the respondent, reflecting the limited impact on grazing and the anticipated community benefit. The respondent, however, has since withdrawn consent and obtained a higher valuation, which the applicants dispute as being inappropriate for the nature of the proposed development. No further compensation is due under the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. No fencing condition is required.

[7] The court is invited to determine whether the statutory criteria for resumption are met and to fix any compensation or share of value due.

Submissions for the respondent

[8] The respondent raised a number of objections, some of which were inconsistent. They are as follows.

[9] The planning permission relied upon by the applicants expired in July 2024. No valid development has commenced. Alternatively, if development has commenced, the application is retrospective, contrary to the Court’s Practice Note No 1.

[10] The application is premature. There is uncertainty over funding and timescales for completion. The applicants have failed to disclose who will operate the Outdoor Hub.

[11] The proposed resumption and facilities are unnecessary. Previous resumptions have already provided facilities in the area, including the Scaladale Centre, which remains underutilised.

[12] The proposed mountain bike trails may extend beyond the resumption site into common grazings and crofter forestry without proper authority. The applicant is not respectful of the rights of the shareholders. One of the applicant’s directors grazed his cattle on the common grazing (contrary to the applicable woodland scheme).

[13] The proposed compensation is inadequate. The subjects, assuming planning permission, have a market value of £65,000. Reference is made to a valuation of the subjects commissioned by the respondent. The respondent is entitled to a share of that value: section 21 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993.

Decision

[14] We are satisfied on the basis of the material before us that the statutory criteria for resumption are met. We authorise resumption in principle. Planning permission has been obtained and, permissibly, initial works have been carried out to preserve the validity of the consent. We are satisfied that these works constitute a valid commencement of development, and accordingly, the planning permission remains extant. The application is not retrospective. The proposed development constitutes a reasonable purpose having relation to the good of the estate or public interest. The development is likely to enhance visitor infrastructure and support responsible outdoor recreation. While other facilities exist in the area, we do not consider these vitiate the reasonableness of the proposed development. The land identified for resumption is not actively grazed, and adequate alternative grazing is available. The development will not prejudice the crofting interests of the respondents and will contribute positively to the local economy (potentially improving employment opportunities) and visitor infrastructure.

[15] While there is no fixed timescale for completion, the applicants have secured initial funding and are actively seeking further support for the main building works. The absence of a definitive completion date does not, in our view, render the application premature.

[16] Turning to the respondent’s complaint that the applicant has failed to disclose who will operate the facilities, the applicant has indicated that it will operate the facilities building and lease the café and retail units to third parties. That is sufficient for present purposes. The applicant is a community‑controlled trust. If the applicant were subsequently to sell the subjects, profits would be reinvested in the community.

[17] The respondent expressed concerns regarding the potential extension of mountain bike trails beyond the resumption site. However, the application relates solely to the delineated area. Any development beyond that boundary is not before the court and would require separate authorisation.

[18] Allegations of unauthorised grazing by a director of the applicant are not directly relevant to the merits of the present application.

[19] We have insufficient information before us to allow us to determine the question of what compensation should be payable. Similarly, we are currently unable to assess the value of the land to be resumed and therefore any share the respondent should receive. The valuation commissioned by the respondent places a market value of £65,000 on the land, assuming residential or commercial use. However, that valuation is no guide to the value of the land taking account of the purpose of the resumption and the planning permission actually obtained and is accordingly irrelevant to the matter at hand.

[20] We shall fix a hearing at which parties can address the court on how compensation and the respondent’s share of the value of the subjects should be assessed. All questions of expenses are reserved.
